name: STM32L562VET6Q
title: STM32L562xx ultra-low-power Arm Cortex-M33 microcontrollers with TrustZone and FPU, 110 MHz, 512 Kbytes Flash, 256 Kbytes SRAM, SMPS, AES and PKA
summary: An ultra-low-power Cortex-M33 microcontroller with Armv8-M TrustZone, a single-precision FPU, DSP instructions and an MPU, running at up to 110 MHz (165 DMIPS) from 1.71 V to 3.6 V. It holds 512 Kbytes of dual-bank Flash with ECC and 256 Kbytes of SRAM (64 Kbytes parity-checked), an 8 Kbyte instruction cache, an Octo-SPI port with on-the-fly decryption, and on 100 pins and up an FSMC. Security hardware covers AES, PKA, HASH, a true RNG, active tamper and secure firmware installation through root secure services. Analog and interfaces include two 12-bit 5 Msps ADCs, two DAC channels, two op-amps, two comparators, USB full-speed device, a Type-C/PD controller, FDCAN, SDMMC, two SAIs, four I2Cs, three SPIs and six U(S)ARTs. Packages with a Q suffix bring out an on-chip SMPS step-down converter. STM32L562VET6Q is the LQFP100 part with the SMPS pinout, -40 to 85 °C ambient, with 79 GPIOs.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, FPU, MPU and DSP instructions, up to 110 MHz, 165 DMIPS, 442 CoreMark
512 Kbytes Flash, two banks read-while-write; 256 Kbytes SRAM (192 + 64 with parity); 512-byte OTP
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; VDDA 1.62 V to 3.6 V; VDDUSB 3.0 V to 3.6 V; VDDIO2 1.08 V to 3.6 V; VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V
106 µA/MHz (LDO); 62 µA/MHz at 3 V with the SMPS
Shutdown 17 nA; Standby 108 nA (222 nA with RTC); Stop 2 with RTC 3.16 µA; VBAT 187 nA
two 12-bit, 5 Msps, up to 16-bit with hardware oversampling, 200 µA/Msps
4 to 48 MHz crystal, 32 kHz crystal, HSI16 ±1%, LSI 32 kHz ±5%, MSI 100 kHz to 48 MHz, HSI48 with clock recovery, 3 PLLs
up to 114 fast I/Os, most 5 V tolerant; up to 14 on an independent supply down to 1.08 V; 79 on LQFP100 SMPS
TrustZone, AES, PKA, HASH, true RNG (NIST SP800-90B), OTFDEC, active tamper, 96-bit unique ID

notes: All parts have 512 Kbytes of Flash (size code E) and 256 Kbytes of system SRAM plus 128 bytes of backup SRAM.

A full order code adds the package letter, the temperature digit (6: -40 to 85 °C ambient, 105 °C junction; 3: -40 to 125 °C ambient, 130 °C junction), the pinout letter and the packing: STM32L562VET6Q is the 100-pin LQFP part for -40 to 85 °C with the SMPS step-down pinout.
USART3 is absent on STM32L562CExxP.

pins.name: VBAT
pins.function: Backup supply, 1.55 V to 3.6 V: RTC, LSE oscillator and backup registers while VDD is absent.

pins.name: PC13
pins.function: FT I/O. Alternate functions: EVENTOUT. Additional: WKUP2, RTC_TS/RTC_OUT1, TAMP_IN1/TAMP_OUT2. Supplied through the backup power switch, which sinks only 3 mA: as an output, at most 2 MHz into 30 pF, and never a current source (no LED drive). After a backup-domain power-up it works as a GPIO; afterwards its role follows the RTC registers, which a system reset does not clear.

circuits.title: SMPS step-down converter supply
circuits.description: Supply hookup for the Q-suffix parts. VDDSMPS takes the same supply as VDD. The converter's switching node VLXSMPS drives a 4.7 µH inductor whose far end is the V15SMPS rail, smoothed by 4.7 µF to VSSSMPS; both V15SMPS pins join that rail and feed the main regulator that makes VCORE.
notes: With the SMPS fitted but never used, VDDSMPS and VLXSMPS go to VSS and V15SMPS to VDD.

circuits.title: 8 MHz crystal on the HSE oscillator
circuits.description: An 8 MHz crystal or resonator between OSC_IN and OSC_OUT, each end loaded by a capacitor to ground. The feedback resistor RF and the gain stage are inside the part. REXT sits in series between the crystal and OSC_OUT and is chosen for the crystal. CL1 and CL2 are ceramic, 5 pF to 20 pF, normally equal; the crystal's rated load is their series value plus about 10 pF of pin and board capacitance.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors takes the place of Y1, C1 and C2.
Crystal and capacitors go as close to the oscillator pins as they can.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal on the LSE oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT with a load capacitor from each pin to ground; the amplifier's drive is set in software (LSEDRV). There is no resistor across the crystal: it is not needed and must not be fitted.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors takes the place of Y1, C1 and C2.
Crystal and capacitors go as close to the oscillator pins as they can.

circuits.title: NRST pin protection
circuits.description: A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, placed close to the part, guards against stray resets, and a push-button to ground gives a manual reset; the pull-up RPU and the filter are inside the part. The external circuit must be able to take NRST below VIL(NRST) max.

circuits.title: ADC input connection
circuits.description: A source VAIN drives an ADC input through its own resistance RAIN, and the board and pad add a parasitic capacitance to ground. RAIN stays within the limit for the chosen resolution and sampling time; a large parasitic capacitance costs accuracy, which a slower ADC clock wins back.
notes: PA0 (ADC12_IN5) stands for any ADC input.

circuits.title: DAC output load
circuits.description: The load a DAC output is specified into: RLOAD and CLOAD in parallel from DAC_OUTx to ground, driven through the output buffer or with the buffer bypassed.
notes: PA4 (DAC1_OUT1) stands for either DAC output.

operation.text: Cortex-M33 at up to 110 MHz with 512 Kbytes of Flash and 256 Kbytes of SRAM, on two APB and two AHB buses joined by a 32-bit multi-AHB matrix. Ratings: -40 to +85 °C ambient (+105 °C junction) or -40 to +125 °C ambient (+130 °C junction), 1.71 V to 3.6 V. Seven packages from 48 to 144 pins; the FSMC exists only on 100 pins and more, and Octo-SPI on all. Separate supplies serve the analog blocks, USB (3.3 V) and up to 14 I/Os (down to 1.08 V); VBAT keeps the RTC and backup registers.

The security model follows Arm TBSA: secure boot, secure storage, secure firmware installation and upgrade. Readout protection has several levels; peripherals, memories and I/Os can be made secure or privileged. Flash and SRAM protections: readout, write, secure and hidden areas. Crypto blocks: AES, PKA, Octo-SPI on-the-fly decryption, HASH and a true RNG. Internal monitors for tamper, temperature, voltage and frequency attacks erase secret data when triggered.

Arm Cortex-M33 implementing Armv8-M Main Extension with TrustZone (secure and non-secure states), single-precision FPU, DSP instructions, MPUs with 8 regions per security state, and a SAU with up to 8 regions. Two bus ports: S-AHB for SRAM, peripherals, external RAM and devices and Vendor_SYS; C-AHB for the code region. Performance: 1.5 DMIPS/MHz (Dhrystone 2.1), 442 CoreMark (4.02 CoreMark/MHz); 370 ULPMark-CP, 54 ULPMark-PP, 27400 SecureMark-TLS.

An 8 Kbyte cache on the C-AHB bus serves fetches from internal and external memory with 0 wait states on a hit. It is 2-way set associative with pLRU-t replacement (or direct mapped, for lower power), refills critical word first with AHB bursts, serves hits during a refill, and has separate master ports for internal (fast bus) and external (slow bus, Octo-SPI/FMC) memory. Up to 4 external regions can be remapped as cacheable. Hit and miss counters, TrustZone support, software coherency maintenance, and an optional interrupt on an unexpected cacheable write.

The MPU confines CPU accesses so that one task cannot corrupt another's memory: up to 8 regions in the secure state and 8 in the non-secure state. A forbidden access can be detected by an RTOS, whose kernel may reprogram the regions per task. Applications that do not need it can leave it bypassed.

512 Kbytes for code and data, single- or dual-bank; dual-bank mode reads one bank while erasing or programming the other and supports dual-bank boot. Each bank has 128 pages of 2 or 4 Kbytes depending on read width. 512 bytes of OTP hold user data. ECC corrects single errors, detects double errors and records the failing address in a register.

Readout protection levels: 0 none; 0.5 only with TrustZone on, where non-secure Flash stays readable and writable and debug may reach non-secure code but not secure code; 1 blocks Flash access while debug is connected or when booting from RAM or the bootloader (with TrustZone on, non-secure debug remains and RAM boot is refused); 2 disables JTAG/SWD debug, RAM boot and bootloader selection for good. Write protection: four areas of 4 Kbyte granularity in single-bank mode, or two per bank of 2 Kbyte granularity in dual-bank mode.

With TrustZone on, all Flash is secure after reset. Watermark option bytes define secure areas (four in single-bank, one per bank in dual-bank, page granularity). A hidden protection area inside the secure area can be locked against reads, writes and fetches until the next reset, so code there runs once. Block-based secure areas let each page be switched secure or non-secure at run time.

256 Kbytes in total: SRAM1, 192 Kbytes at 0x2000 0000, and SRAM2, 64 Kbytes with hardware parity at 0x0A03 0000, also mapped at 0x2003 0000 to run on from SRAM1. SRAM2 sits on the C-bus; all 64 Kbytes or the top 4 Kbytes can be kept in Standby, and it can be write-protected in 1 Kbyte steps. Access is at CPU speed with 0 wait states. With TrustZone on, all SRAM is secure after reset; the GTZC MPCBB makes 256-byte blocks non-secure.

The PH3-BOOT0 pin (or an option bit, freeing the pad as a GPIO), nBOOT0, and the NSBOOTADDx[24:0] or SECBOOTADD0[24:0] option bytes choose the boot address: anywhere in user Flash, the system bootloader, anywhere in SRAM, or the root secure services (RSS). The bootloader in system memory reprograms Flash over USART, I2C, SPI, FDCAN or USB FS (DFU) and is present on every device. RSS, programmed by ST in the secure information block and reachable once TZEN is set, supports secure firmware installation (RSSe SFI). With TrustZone on, booting must be secure and uses SECBOOTADD0; BOOT_LOCK forces every boot to that address. If a programmed boot address is outside the allowed area at RDP 0.5 or higher, boot falls back to 0x0800 0000 (TZEN = 0) or RSS (TZEN = 1).

Three sub-blocks, each with its own 32-bit AHB interface: TZSC sets the secure and privileged state of peripherals and masters and the non-secure size of watermark memory regions (MPCWM), and tells RCC and GPIO which peripherals are secure; MPCBB sets the security of each 256-byte SRAM block; TZIC collects illegal-access events and raises a secure interrupt. MPCBB and TZIC accept only secure transactions.

TZEN in FLASH_OPTR turns TrustZone on. The SAU (up to 8 regions) and the fixed IDAU then decide each address's security; the stricter result wins. Flash, system SRAM and peripherals appear twice, at secure and non-secure aliases; external memories have one alias. Peripherals are either securable (behind a TZSC-controlled AHB/APB gate) or TrustZone-aware (with their own secure registers).

After reset: the CPU is secure and must boot from a secure address; the SAU makes the whole map secure; Flash security follows the watermark options and block-based Flash is non-secure; all SRAM and MPCBB are secure; FSMC and Octo-SPI banks and MPCWMx are secure; securable peripherals and TrustZone-aware peripherals (bar GPIO) are non-secure, though the latter's secure configuration registers are secure; every GPIO is secure; NVIC interrupts are all secure (NVIC is banked); TZIC illegal-access interrupts are off.

VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V feeds the I/Os, regulator and system analog. VDDA (1.62 V for ADC and COMP, 1.8 V for DAC and OPAMP, 2.4 V for VREFBUF, up to 3.6 V) feeds the analog blocks and is best tied to VDD when they are unused. VDDSMPS 1.71 V to 3.6 V feeds the SMPS and shares VDD's source; VLXSMPS is its switched output and V15SMPS takes the converter output to the regulator (SMPS packages only). VDD12 1.05 V to 1.32 V bypasses the regulator from an external SMPS (P packages only), with no decoupling and no load. VDDUSB 3.0 V to 3.6 V feeds the USB transceivers. VDDIO2 1.08 V to 3.6 V feeds PG[15:2]. VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V keeps the RTC, LSE and backup registers when VDD is gone. VCORE, from the internal regulator, supplies the digital logic and SRAM; Flash takes VCORE and VDD.

VREF+ is the ADC and DAC reference and the VREFBUF output. With VDDA < 2 V it must equal VDDA; with VDDA ≥ 2 V it lies between 2 V and VDDA; it may be grounded while ADC and DAC are off. VREFBUF gives about 2.048 V (needs VDDA ≥ 2.4 V) or about 2.5 V (needs VDDA ≥ 2.8 V), chosen by VRS in VREFBUF_CSR. On packages without VREF pins they are bonded to VSSA and VDDA; where VREF+ is double-bonded with VDDA, VREFBUF must stay off. VREF- always equals VSSA.

While VDD is under 1 V, VDDA, VDDIO2 and VDDUSB must stay below VDD + 300 mV. Above 1 V the supplies are independent. During power-down VDD may briefly fall below the others only if the energy delivered to the device stays under 1 mJ, letting decoupling capacitors discharge at different rates.

An ultra-low-power brownout reset works in every mode except Shutdown and holds the device in reset below threshold, with no external reset part needed; its lowest level is 1.71 V at power-on and option bytes select higher ones. The software-enabled PVD compares VDD with VPVD and can interrupt on falling below and/or rising above it. Peripheral voltage monitors check VDDA, VDDUSB and VDDIO2 against fixed thresholds. Temperature thresholds and an upper VDD threshold are also monitored.

The main regulator (MR) runs in Run, Sleep and Stop 0; the low-power regulator (LPR) in Stop 1, Stop 2 and both low-power run and sleep modes, and holds SRAM2 (64 or 4 Kbytes) in Standby with retention. Both are off, output high-impedance, in Standby and Shutdown. Dynamic voltage scaling sets VCORE by speed: Range 0 up to 110 MHz, Range 1 up to 80 MHz, Range 2 up to 26 MHz with every peripheral clock also at most 26 MHz. Low-power run takes VCORE from the LPR with the CPU at up to 2 MHz.

On Q packages an on-chip switching step-down converter feeds the regulator, saving power when VDD is high enough. It drops into bypass automatically when VDD falls below 2 V in Range 0 and Range 1, but not in Range 2. Modes: high-power (default after POR, best at heavy load), low-power (best at light load) and bypass, which software may select at any time, leaving the main regulator alone. External parts: 4.7 µH between VLXSMPS and V15SMPS, 4.7 µF from V15SMPS to VSSSMPS. If the SMPS is never used, VDDSMPS and VLXSMPS go to VSS and V15SMPS to VDD. After POR it starts in high-power, slow-start mode to limit inrush; setting SMPSFSTEN in PWR_CR4 selects a fast start for the next system reset or wakeup (not from Shutdown or VBAT).

Run is the state after reset. Sleep stops only the CPU. Low-power run supplies VCORE from the LPR with the CPU at up to 2 MHz, running from SRAM or Flash; independently clocked peripherals may use HSI16. Low-power sleep stops the CPU clock from Low-power run and returns there on wakeup. Stop 0, 1 and 2 keep SRAM and registers but stop all VCORE clocks and turn off PLL, MSI, HSI16 and HSE; LSE or LSI keep running and the RTC may stay active; some wakeup-capable peripherals can switch HSI16 on to detect their event. Stop 2 puts most of VCORE in low leakage; Stop 1 keeps more peripherals and wakes faster; Stop 0 keeps the main regulator on for the fastest wakeup at much higher current. The clock on leaving Stop is MSI up to 48 MHz or HSI16.

Standby turns the regulator, VCORE, PLL, MSI, HSI16 and HSE off; the RTC may stay on and the BOR stays active (BORL may be set to ultra-low-power). Each I/O can be pulled up, pulled down or left floating. SRAM1 and registers are lost except the backup domain and standby circuitry; SRAM2, whole or 4 Kbytes, may be kept on the LPR. Exit on NRST, IWDG reset, a WKUP pin edge, an RTC event (alarm, periodic wakeup, timestamp, tamper) or an LSE failure; the clock is then MSI up to 8 MHz. Shutdown also stops LSI and has no BOR or supply monitoring, so the switch to the backup domain is not supported; SRAM and registers are lost except the backup domain. Exit on NRST, a WKUP edge or an RTC event; the clock is then MSI at 4 MHz.
During and after reset, I/Os sit in analog state with their Schmitt triggers off to save current, and the reset pull-up is switched off when the reset comes from inside the device.

VBAT can come from a battery, a supercapacitor, or VDD when no battery is fitted. It supplies the RTC with the LSE and the backup registers; three tamper pins work in VBAT mode. The device switches to VBAT automatically when VDD disappears, and an internal charger can charge the VBAT element while VDD is present. Running from VBAT, neither external interrupts nor RTC events take the device out of VBAT operation.

With TZEN set, the low-power mode, WKUP pin, voltage detection and VBAT settings can be made secure. Further PWR bits become secure when the matching resource is: VOS once RCC holds the SYSCLK selection secure, a GPIO's Standby pull-up/down bit when that GPIO is secure, and the backup write-protect bit when the RTC is secure.
Peripherals signal one another directly, without the CPU, with fixed latency. Depending on the link, some of these links stay active down to Stop 2.

SYSCLK comes from one of four sources: HSE, a 4 to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator (or bypassed external clock); HSI16, a trimmable 16 MHz RC; MSI, a trimmable RC with 12 steps from 100 kHz to 48 MHz that the LSE can trim automatically to better than ±0.25%, good enough to clock USB without a crystal; or the system PLL (from HSE, HSI16 or MSI, up to 110 MHz). HSI48 serves USB, SDMMC and RNG and can be output on MCO. The UCPD kernel clock derives from HSI16, which must be on first. The RTC runs from the 32.768 kHz LSE (four drive strengths, or bypass) or the 32 kHz LSI (±5%, also clocking the IWDG, divisible by 128 to 250 Hz). Three PLLs, each with three outputs, clock the ADC, USB/SDMMC/RNG and the SAIs independently. After reset the MSI runs at 4 MHz. The CSS switches to HSI16 and may interrupt if the HSE fails; an LSE failure can also be detected. MCO outputs an internal clock; LSCO outputs LSI or LSE in every low-power mode except VBAT. AHB, APB1 and APB2 run at up to 110 MHz.

With TZEN set, RCC can protect from non-secure access the configuration and status of every oscillator (HSE and LSE with their CSS, HSI, MSI, LSI, HSI48), the PLLs and AHB prescaler, the SYSCLK and HSI48 source selection, the MCO setup with STOPWUCK, and the RMVF reset-flag bit. A secure peripheral's clock, reset, source selection and low-power enable bits are secure too.
Trims HSI48 automatically against a sync source: USB SOF, the LSE, a signal on CRS_SYNC, or software. Manual trimming can be added for faster lock at start-up.

Each pin is configurable as push-pull or open-drain output, input with or without pull-up/pull-down, or alternate function; most share digital or analog functions. After reset every GPIO is in analog mode. A locking sequence can freeze the alternate-function setup. Each pin can be made secure, protecting its mode, alternate function and data bits from non-secure software; all ports are secure after reset.
A 32-bit multi-AHB matrix links the masters (CPU, DMA1, DMA2, SDMMC1) to the slaves (Flash, SRAM1, SRAM2, FMC, Octo-SPI, AHB and APB peripherals) so that several fast masters can work at once.

Two DMA controllers with 8 channels each, 16 in all, each channel serving peripheral requests or software-triggered memory-to-memory transfers. Four software priority levels per channel, ties broken by request number. Source and destination sizes (byte, half-word, word) are independent, with packing and unpacking; addresses align to data size. Circular buffers, 0 to 2^18 - 1 items per transfer, and an interrupt per channel on transfer complete, half transfer or error. Secure and non-secure transfers are set per channel and separately for source and destination; privileged and unprivileged transfers per channel.

Routes 90 peripheral request lines to 16 output channels, each with its own synchronization input selector, request counter, overrun flag and an event output for chaining. A 4-channel request generator takes 23 trigger inputs; 23 synchronization inputs. Secure, non-secure, privileged and unprivileged transfers are set per channel, with separate secure and non-secure interrupts.

8 priority levels, up to 109 maskable interrupt channels plus the Cortex-M33's 16 lines; low latency with late-arrival handling, tail chaining and automatic state saving. NVIC registers are banked between secure and non-secure states.

43 event inputs, all able to wake the system from Stop, routed to the power controller, the NVIC and the CPU event input (through an event generator). Configurable events (from I/Os or pulse-producing peripherals) have selectable edges, separate rising and falling pending bits, masks and a software trigger. Direct events (from peripherals with their own flag) are rising-edge only, without EXTI pending bit or software trigger. Secure inputs' control bits can be made secure. EXTI also holds the I/O port selection.
Computes a CRC with a configurable polynomial and size, for example to check Flash integrity under EN/IEC 60335-1 or to compare a run-time signature of the software with one made at link time.

Static memory controller (also called FMC) with a NOR/PSRAM controller and a NAND controller: SRAM, NOR/OneNAND Flash, PSRAM in four banks, NAND with hardware ECC over up to 8 Kbytes, and FRAM; 8- or 16-bit bus; a chip select and configuration per bank; write FIFO. It drives graphic LCD controllers in Intel 8080 and Motorola 6800 modes. With TrustZone on, all banks start secure; MPCWM2 opens up to two non-secure NOR/PSRAM areas in 64 Kbyte steps, MPCWM3 makes the NAND bank wholly secure or non-secure, and TZSC can make its registers secure.

Interface for single, dual, quad or octal SPI memories, in classical frames (command, address, alternate bytes, dummy cycles, data on 1, 2, 4 or 8 lines) or HyperBus frames. Modes: indirect, status polling, and memory-mapped with read and write. Dual-quad mode, SDR and DTR, data strobe, programmable opcode and frame format, FIFO, 8/16/32-bit access, DMA in indirect mode, timeout, and interrupts on FIFO threshold, timeout, status match, completion and access error. With TrustZone on, the bank starts secure and MPCWM1 opens up to two non-secure areas in 64 Kbyte steps.

Two 12-bit SAR converters with built-in calibration: 5.33 Msps at full resolution, sampling time down to 18.75 ns, up to 8.88 Msps at 6 bits. Up to 16 external channels plus 5 internal (VREFINT, temperature sensor, VBAT/3, DAC1 outputs); single-ended or differential inputs; an external reference pin on some packages. Current falls linearly with conversion rate, and the ADC clock is independent of the CPU. Sequencer with regular and injected groups, single, continuous or discontinuous scan, timer and external triggers, DMA, alignment and per-channel offset, hardware oversampling, per-channel sampling time, analog watchdog driving interrupts and timer triggers, and injected-context queueing.

Produces a voltage linear in temperature on ADC1_IN17. Its offset varies from chip to chip, so uncalibrated it suits only relative measurements; each device carries factory calibration values in read-only system memory (TS_CAL1 at 30 °C, TS_CAL2 at 130 °C).
A bandgap reference for the ADC and comparators, on ADC1_IN0, measured on each part in production with the value kept in read-only system memory.
ADC1_IN18 reads VBAT through an internal divide-by-3 bridge, since VBAT may exceed VDDA.

Two 12-bit buffered output channels built from resistor strings and an inverting amplifier: 8- or 12-bit mode, factory and user buffer-offset trimming, left or right alignment, synchronized update, noise and triangle wave generation, independent or simultaneous dual conversion, DMA per channel, external triggers (timer update outputs), and a low-power sample-and-hold mode with internal or external capacitor.

A reference buffer driving the ADC, DACs and, through VREF+, external parts, at 2.048 V or 2.5 V. With the buffer off, an external reference can be applied on VREF+. Packages that double-bond VREF+ to VDDA have no VREFBUF. A 100 nF capacitor on VREF+ sets its low-frequency cut-off.

Two comparators, rail to rail, whose reference is selectable (external I/O, DAC outputs, or VREFINT and its 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 fractions), hysteresis, speed and output polarity. Both wake the device from Stop, raise interrupts and timer breaks, and can pair as a window comparator.
Two op-amps, each usable as a follower routed inside or outside the chip, or as a built-in PGA: low input bias current, low offset, a low-power mode and rail-to-rail input.

Four digital filters with eight external serial inputs (or eight internal parallel inputs) for external sigma-delta modulators and PDM microphones, converting PDM to PCM in hardware. Serial inputs use SPI or Manchester 1-wire formats with a clock output for the modulators; parallel inputs take up to 16-bit data from the ADCs or memory. Sinc filter of order 1 to 5 with oversampling up to 1024, integrator oversampling 1 to 256, output up to 24 bits with a 0 to 31-bit right shift, signed, with offset correction. Conversion starts by software, timers, external events or in step with filter 0. An analog watchdog with its own sinc filter (order 1 to 3, oversampling 1 to 32), a short-circuit detector counting 1 to 256 identical bits, break outputs, min/max detector, DMA, and regular or injected conversions.

Surface charge-transfer capacitive sensing for keys, sliders, wheels and proximity: up to 22 channels, up to 3 acquired in parallel with one sampling capacitor per group, spread spectrum, hardware-sequenced acquisition, programmable charge-transfer frequency, sampling and channel pins, a max-count limit for faulty channels, and end-of-acquisition and max-count interrupts. Channel count depends on package and free I/Os. Used with the STMTouch library.

An analog entropy source with NIST SP800-90B approved conditioning, giving 32-bit samples, usable as the entropy source of a non-deterministic random bit generator. Four 32-bit samples every 412 AHB cycles when fAHB < 77 MHz, or every 256 RNG clock cycles otherwise. Health tests at start-up and continuously (adaptive proportion, repetition count), with error handling. It can be disabled or left in its default automatic low-power mode. Register access is by 32-bit words only; other accesses raise an AHB bus error and writes are ignored.

FIPS 197 AES encryption and decryption with 128- or 256-bit keys on 128-bit blocks: ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM, GMAC and CMAC modes, key scheduling and decryption-key derivation, a 128-bit initialization vector or counter register, 32-bit input and output buffers with 32-bit register access, two DMA channels (in and out), and suspension of a message for a higher-priority one.
Hardware SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256 and MD5 with HMAC, giving 160, 224, 256 or 128-bit digests of messages up to 2^64 - 1 bits; HMAC calls the hash twice.

Computes RSA, Diffie-Hellman and ECC over GF(p) in the Montgomery domain, with the domain transforms built in: RSA modular exponentiation and CRT exponentiation, ECC scalar multiplication and point-on-curve check, ECDSA signing and verification, plus modular add, subtract, multiply, reduce, invert and compare. Operand size limit: 3136 bits (RSA, DH), 640 bits (ECC). 32-bit word access only; other writes raise an AHB bus error and are ignored.

Decrypts, with no added latency, encrypted Octo-SPI memory read in memory-mapped mode, using AES-128 in counter mode on 8- to 512-bit reads. Up to four regions of 4096-byte granularity, each with its own 128-bit key, two-byte firmware version and fixed 64-bit nonce, a keystream tied to the system address, a lock on region setup, and an option to decrypt instruction fetches only. Keys sit in write-only, lockable registers. A 2-deep keystream FIFO supports Octo-SPI prefetch, and an enhanced mode adds a proprietary layer over the AES stream.
Timer set: TIM1 and TIM8 (advanced control), up to nine general-purpose, TIM6 and TIM7 (basic), the LPTIMs, IWDG, WWDG and SysTick.

Each is a three-phase PWM generator on six outputs with complementary outputs and programmable dead time, or a full general-purpose timer. Four channels for input capture, output compare, edge- or centre-aligned PWM (0 to 100%) and one-pulse output. In debug the counter can freeze and the outputs shut off to protect power switches. They synchronize or chain with the other timers through Timer Link.

TIM2 and TIM5: 32-bit up/down counters with 32-bit prescaler; TIM3 and TIM4: 16-bit up/down counters with 16-bit prescaler; all four have four channels for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse, quadrature encoder support, independent DMA and debug freeze, and link with other timers. TIM15 (two channels, one complementary), TIM16 and TIM17 (one channel, one complementary) have 16-bit upcounters and prescalers, DMA, Timer Link and debug freeze.
16-bit time bases, chiefly for triggering the DAC.

Independently clocked; running from LSE, LSI or an external clock, each keeps counting in Stop and can wake the device. LPTIM1 and LPTIM3 work in Stop 0, 1 and 2; LPTIM2 in Stop 0 and 1. 16-bit upcounter with autoreload and compare, pulse or PWM output, continuous or one-shot, software or hardware trigger, clock from LSE, LSI, HSI16, APB or an external input (counting even with no internal clock running), a digital glitch filter, and encoder mode on LPTIM1.

IWDG: 12-bit downcounter with 8-bit prescaler on the 32 kHz LSI, so it runs in Stop and Standby; resets the device or serves as a free-running timeout timer; hardware or software start by option bytes; freezable in debug. WWDG: 7-bit downcounter on the main clock with an early-warning interrupt, freezable in debug.

Two SysTick timers, secure and non-secure, when TrustZone is on; one otherwise. Each is a 24-bit downcounter with autoreload, an interrupt at zero and a selectable clock, meant for an RTOS or as a plain down counter.

BCD calendar with subseconds, 12- or 24-hour time, weekday, date, month and year, with automatic month-length and leap-year handling; two alarms; shift correction of 1 to 32767 RTC clock pulses; 50/60 Hz reference clock detection; digital calibration in 0.95 ppm steps; timestamps on the timestamp pin, a tamper event or a switch to VBAT; a 17-bit auto-reload wakeup timer. Fully securable, with alarms, wakeup timer and timestamp each secure or not. Powered from VDD or VBAT through a switch. Clock: LSE crystal, resonator or oscillator, LSI, or HSE through a prescaler. On LSE it runs in VBAT and every low-power mode; on LSI it runs in every low-power mode but Shutdown and not in VBAT. Every RTC event can interrupt and wake the device.

32 backup registers of 32 bits, kept in every low-power mode and in VBAT, erasable on any tamper detection. 8 external tamper pins (edge, filtered or unfiltered level, or active mode that checks the pins are neither open nor shorted; passive inputs have a configurable filter and pull-up) and 5 internal tamper events; any detection can also take an RTC timestamp. The backup registers split into three adjustable areas: secure read/write, secure write with non-secure read, and non-secure read/write. A monotonic counter is included.

Four I2C interfaces handling sequencing, protocol, arbitration and timing: master, slave and multimaster; Standard-mode to 100 kbit/s, Fast-mode to 400 kbit/s, Fast-mode Plus to 1 Mbit/s with 20 mA drive I/Os; 7- or 10-bit addresses, several 7-bit slave addresses, programmable hold and setup times; optional clock stretching. SMBus 2.0 (hardware PEC, ARP, alert) and PMBus 1.1. Independent kernel clock, analog and digital noise filters, a 1-byte buffer with DMA. All wake from Stop 0/1 on address match; I2C3 also from Stop 2.

USART1 to USART3 and UART4, UART5: asynchronous links up to 10 Mbit/s with IrDA SIR, multiprocessor mode, single-wire half duplex, LIN, CTS/RTS flow control and RS485 driver enable; the USARTs add ISO 7816 smartcard and SPI-like synchronous modes. Their clock domain is separate from the CPU's, so they wake the device from Stop at up to 200 Kbaud on a start bit, any frame or a chosen frame. All work with DMA.

One low-power UART with half-duplex single wire, CTS/RTS and multiprocessor mode. On its own clock it wakes the device from Stop at up to 220 Kbaud on a start bit, any frame or a chosen frame; with only the 32.768 kHz LSE it runs up to 9600 baud, so it can wait for frames in Stop at very low energy. Faster clocks reach higher rates. DMA capable.

Three SPIs in master or slave, full duplex, half duplex or simplex; a 3-bit prescaler gives eight master clock rates; frames of 4 to 16 bits; hardware CRC, TI mode and NSS pulse mode; DMA capable. With the USARTs and Octo-SPI in SPI mode, up to seven SPIs.

Two serial audio interfaces, each with two independent sub-blocks that transmit or receive through 8-word FIFOs, synchronous or asynchronous to each other, master or slave each, with a clock generator per sub-block. Data of 8, 10, 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits; protocols I2S, PCM/DSP, TDM, AC'97, SPDIF output and LSB- or MSB-justified; up to 16 slots with selectable active ones; configurable frame length, sync level, offset and width, first-bit position, LSB or MSB first, clock edge, mute, stereo/mono; error flags for overrun/underrun, early or late frame sync and codec not ready; DMA per sub-block. PDM only on SAI1.

SD, SDIO and MMC host: MMC 4.51 with 1-, 4- and 8-bit buses, SD memory 4.1, SDIO 4.0 with 1- and 4-bit buses (SDR104 clock capped by the I/O speed; no SPI or UHS-II mode), up to 104 Mbyte/s in 8-bit mode depending on I/O speed, and direction signals for external bus drivers.
One CAN controller to ISO 11898-1 (CAN 2.0 A and B) and CAN FD 1.0, with 1 Kbyte of message RAM for filters, receive FIFOs and buffers, transmit event FIFO and transmit buffers.

USB 2.0 full-speed (12 Mbit/s) device with internal PHY, built-in DP pull-up, battery charging detection to BCD 1.2, link power management, configurable endpoints with up to 1 Kbyte packet memory, and suspend/resume. It needs an exact 48 MHz clock: from the main PLL with an HSE crystal, or from HSI48 trimmed automatically from USB SOF, which removes the crystal.

One controller to USB Type-C 1.2 and USB PD 3.0 using dedicated I/Os with Rp (all values) and Rd resistors, dead-battery support, PD message transmit and receive and fast role swap. The logic debounces Type-C levels with interrupts, detects FRS, offers a byte interface for PD payloads with DMA, timing dividers, CRC, 4b5b coding, ordered sets with a receive mask, and frequency recovery on the preamble. It keeps detecting PD messages and FRS in Stop mode.

SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial wire debug; SWD needs two pins, with TMS/SWDIO and TCK/SWCLK shared and a TMS sequence switching between JTAG-DP and SW-DP; the other JTAG pins can be GPIOs. The Embedded Trace Macrocell streams compressed instruction and data trace over a few ETM pins to an external trace port analyzer.

Every voltage is measured from VSS unless a table says otherwise. Minimum and maximum figures hold over the worst case of ambient temperature, supply voltage and frequency; they are tested on every device in production at TA = 25 °C and at TA = TAmax of the chosen temperature range. Figures that come from characterization, design simulation or technology data are marked in the table notes and are not tested in production; characterized minimum and maximum figures are the sample mean ±3σ. Typical figures are at TA = 25 °C and VDD = VDDA = 3 V unless stated, are design guidance and are not tested. Typical ADC accuracy figures come from a sample batch of one diffusion lot measured across all temperatures, with 95% of devices at or below the figure (mean ±2σ). Typical curves are design guidance and are not tested. Pin parameters are measured with a 50 pF load from the pin to ground, and a pin's input voltage is taken between the pin and ground.

VDD supplies the I/O ring (VDDIO1), the GPIOs and the regulator that makes VCORE for the CPU, digital logic and memories. The backup domain (LSE, RTC, backup registers) runs from VBAT, 1.55 V to 3.6 V, through a power switch. VDDIO2 supplies its own group of GPIOs through level shifters. VDDA and VREF+ feed the ADCs, DACs, op-amps, comparators and VREFBUF, returned to VSSA and VREF-. Decoupling: n × 100 nF plus one 4.7 µF on the VDD pins; m × 100 nF plus 4.7 µF on the VDDIO2 pins; 10 nF plus 1 µF on VDDA; 100 nF plus 1 µF on VREF+. Every supply pair (VDD/VSS, VDDA/VSSA and so on) needs its ceramic capacitors as near the pins as possible, or under them on the far side of the board.

operation.topic: Supply scheme of P packages (external SMPS)
operation.text: The P parts add two VDD12 pins through which an external SMPS can supply the core directly at 1.05 V to 1.32 V. When the embedded LDO is used instead of an external SMPS, the VDD12 pins are left unconnected.

operation.topic: Supply scheme of Q packages (internal SMPS)
operation.text: The Q parts add the step-down converter pins VDDSMPS, VLXSMPS, two V15SMPS and VSSSMPS; the converter's output feeds the regulator. A Q part whose SMPS is never used has VDDSMPS and VLXSMPS tied to VSS and V15SMPS tied to VDD.

The IDD_ALL figures of the supply-current tables are the whole device current: the sum of the currents into VDD, VDDIO2, VDDA, VDDUSB, VBAT and, on parts with the SMPS, VDDSMPS. IDD_VBAT is the current into VBAT alone.

The figures of the voltage, current and thermal tables are stress limits; going past them can damage the device permanently, and operation at them is not implied. Long exposure to the limits can reduce reliability. Qualification is to JEDEC JESD47 for the application mission profile; longer mission profiles can be asked for.

The internal step-down converter needs a 4.7 µH (typical) inductor from VLXSMPS to the V15SMPS pins and a 4.7 µF (typical) capacitor from V15SMPS to VSSSMPS; VDDSMPS takes VDD. Its mode depends on the regulator range, VDD and the load, as the SMPS modes table gives. In Range 2 there is no automatic bypass: software watches VDD with PVD0 and asks for bypass mode itself. Below 2.05 V on VDDSMPS the hardware forces bypass in Range 0 and Range 1.

Supply current depends on supply voltage, ambient temperature, I/O loading, software configuration, clock frequencies, I/O switching rate, where the program runs from and the code itself. It is measured as the total device current (see Current consumption measurement) with every I/O in analog input mode, every peripheral off unless the table says otherwise, the Flash wait states set to the minimum for fHCLK (RM0438 gives the table), fPCLK = fHCLK when peripherals are on, and the voltage range set by frequency: Range 0 for 80 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 110 MHz, Range 1 for 26 MHz < fHCLK ≤ 80 MHz, Range 2 for fHCLK ≤ 26 MHz. Ambient temperature and supply voltage are as in the general operating conditions.

An input with its pull-up draws current whenever the pin is held low from outside; the pull-up and pull-down values are in the I/O static characteristics. Outputs also carry any external pull-down or load. An input held at an intermediate level draws current through its Schmitt trigger; configuring unused or ADC pins as analog avoids it. A floating input can drift to an intermediate level or toggle from noise, so a pin is set to analog mode, given a pull-up or pull-down, or made an output.

A switching I/O draws current from its I/O supply to run the pin circuitry and to charge and discharge the load on the pin; it adds to the internal peripheral current. It is measured with the pin in push-pull output mode toggled by software at a fixed frequency.

Each peripheral current figure is the device current with that peripheral clocked minus the current with it unclocked, with every I/O in analog mode, at the ambient temperature and supply voltage of the voltage characteristics. It covers the digital part only; the analog parts are given with each analog peripheral.
Each wakeup time runs from the wakeup event to the first user instruction executed. The device enters the low-power mode on a WFE instruction.
With HSE or LSE in bypass, the oscillator is off and its input pin acts as an ordinary GPIO input fed by the outside clock, which must meet the I/O characteristics.

HSE runs from a 4 MHz to 48 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator. The figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. Resonator and load capacitors sit as near the oscillator pins as possible, which keeps output distortion and start-up settling down. CL1 and CL2 are good ceramic capacitors for high-frequency use, typically 5 pF to 20 pF, normally of equal value, chosen for the crystal: the load the crystal maker specifies is CL1 and CL2 in series, plus the pin and board capacitance (about 10 pF combined as a first guess). REXT depends on the crystal.

LSE runs from a 32.768 kHz crystal. The figures come from design simulation with typical external parts. Crystal and load capacitors sit as near the oscillator pins as possible. No resistor goes between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT: none is needed and fitting one is not allowed.
Internal clock figures hold over the ambient temperature and supply range of the general operating conditions; the curves are characterization results, not production tested.

Susceptibility is tested on samples during characterization, with the part running a small program that toggles two LEDs. ESD pulses of both polarities go to every pin until the program is disturbed (IEC 61000-4-2), and fast transient bursts of both polarities go to VDD and VSS through 100 pF (IEC 61000-4-4). A reset brings the part back to normal running. Levels and classes follow ST application note AN1709.

EMC results depend heavily on the application and its software, so EMC-aware software and pre-qualification at the needed level are advised. Software should recover from a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset and corrupted critical data such as control registers. Most such failures can be reproduced by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for one second, and ESD can be applied to the part within its rated range; ST application note AN1015 covers hardening.

ESD: a positive and then a negative pulse, one second apart, go to each pin combination of each sample; the sample count is 3 parts × (n+1) supply pins (ANSI/JEDEC). Latch-up: on three parts, each supply pin is over-driven and current is injected into every I/O and signal pin, to EIA/JESD 78E.

Driving an I/O pin below VSS or above VDDIOx injects current and is to be avoided in normal use. Robustness is tested on samples: current is injected into one floating-input pin at a time while a program runs, and a fault is an ADC error above 5 LSB TUE, induced leakage on neighbouring pins outside -5 µA to +0 µA, a reset, or an oscillator frequency shift. Negative injection causes negative induced leakage, positive injection positive leakage.

Every I/O meets CMOS and TTL input levels without any software setting; the thresholds of the static characteristics cover both, and are tested in production where the CMOS requirement applies and set by simulation elsewhere.

A GPIO sinks or sources up to ±8 mA, or up to ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH. The total sourced by the I/Os on VDDIOx plus the MCU's own VDD current must stay within ΣIVDD, and the total sunk through VSS plus the MCU's own VSS current within ΣIVSS, of the voltage characteristics.

Rise and fall times are taken between 10% and 90% of the swing. The maximum frequency holds when tr + tf ≤ 2/3 of the period and the duty cycle stays within 45% to 55%, with the specified load capacitance.

The NRST input stage is CMOS with a permanent internal pull-up RPU. A 0.1 µF capacitor from NRST to ground, mounted close to the part, keeps stray resets out. Whatever drives NRST must pull it below VIL(NRST) max, or the reset is ignored.
A pulse on an interrupt input must last at least PLEC for the event controller to catch it.

The ADC figures are preliminary, over the temperature, fPCLK and VDDA range of the general operating conditions. A calibration after every power-up is advised. The analog switch booster is on (BOOSTEN = 1 in SYSCFG_CFGR1) while VDDA < 2.4 V and off from 2.4 V up. Depending on the package, VREF+ may be tied to VDDA and VREF- to VSSA inside. The fast channels are PC0, PC1, PC2, PC3 and PA0; every other ADC input is slow.

ET, the total unadjusted error, is the largest gap between the real and the ideal transfer curves. EO, the offset error, is the gap between the first real transition and the first ideal one. EG, the gain error, is the gap between the last ideal transition and the last real one. ED, the differential linearity error, is the largest gap between a real step and an ideal step. EL, the integral linearity error, is the largest gap between any real transition and the line joining the end points.

The source drives the input through its own resistance RAIN, kept within the RAIN limit for the resolution and sampling time; the internal sample capacitor is CADC. Board and pad capacitance (Cparasitic, pad 5 pF) lowers accuracy, which a lower fADC recovers. Supplies are decoupled as the power supply scheme shows, with the 10 nF capacitor a good ceramic part right at the chip.
The DAC has an output buffer that lowers the output impedance so DAC_OUTx can drive a load directly, with no external op-amp. Setting BOFFx in DAC_CR bypasses it.
For tamper detection the part watches for a high or a low temperature and for a high VDD, either continuously or periodically with a minimum on-time TPWMon.
DFSDM timings hold over the temperature, fAPB2 and VDD range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 10, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD.
Timer figures are guaranteed by design; the input and output pins follow the I/O port characteristics.

The I2C interface meets the timing of the I2C-bus specification rev. 03 in Standard-mode (up to 100 kbit/s), Fast-mode (up to 400 kbit/s) and Fast-mode Plus (up to 1 Mbit/s), guaranteed by design when the peripheral is set up correctly. SDA and SCL are not true open-drain: in open-drain mode the PMOS to VDDIOx is turned off but still present. Only FT_f pins meet the Fm+ low-level output current. Every SDA and SCL pin has an analog spike filter.

SPI timings hold over the temperature, fPCLKx and supply range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD; the timing diagrams take levels at 0.3 VDD and 0.7 VDD.

SAI timings hold over the temperature, fPCLKx and VDD range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 10, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD. The APB clock must be at least twice the SAI clock.
FDCAN_TX and FDCAN_RX follow the I/O port characteristics.
USART synchronous timings hold over the temperature, fPCLKx and VDD range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD.

FMC timings hold over the temperature, fHCLK and VDD range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD. THCLK is the HCLK period. The asynchronous figures use ADDSET = 0x1, ADDHLD = 0x1, NBLSET = 0x1, DATAST = 0x1 (0x5 in asynchronous NWAIT mode), DATAHLD = 0x1 (one THCLK for reads, two for writes) and BusTurnAroundDuration = 0x0, with CL = 30 pF.

The synchronous figures use burst access enabled, memory type CRAM, write burst enabled, CLKDivision = 1 and DataLatency = 1 for NOR Flash or 0 for PSRAM. FMC_CLK reaches 55 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x1 and 42 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x0 at 2.7 V to 3.6 V, and 55 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x1 and 26 MHz with CLKDIV = 0x0 at 1.71 V to 1.9 V with CL = 20 pF. R is the clock ratio, HCLK period over FMC_CLK period.

The NAND figures use, for both common and attribute space, SetupTime = 0x01, WaitSetupTime = 0x03, HoldSetupTime = 0x02 and HiZSetupTime = 0x01, on the NAND bank with a 16-bit data width, ECC on with 512-byte pages, and TCLRSetupTime = TARSetupTime = 0. ALE is FMC_A17 and CLE is FMC_A16.

OCTOSPI timings hold over the temperature, fAHB and VDD range of the general operating conditions with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11; for DTR with DQS and HyperBus the delay is set to DLYCFGR[3:0] = 4. The figures apply to both octal and quad SPI modes.
The delay block's figures hold over the temperature, fPCLKx and VDD range of the general operating conditions.

SDMMC timings hold over the temperature, fPCLKx and VDD range of the general operating conditions, with OSPEEDRy[1:0] = 11, a 30 pF load and measurement at 0.5 × VDD. SD at 1.8 V needs an external voltage converter.
The UCPD controller follows the Type-C specification at revision 1.2 and the Power Delivery specification at revision 3.0.

Each package carries the product identification, a date code (year and week, Y WW) and a revision code R beside the pin 1 or ball A1 mark; examples are STM32L562 / CET6 (LQFP48), STM32L562 / CEU6 (UFQFPN48), STM32L562 / RET6P (LQFP64), L562ME6P (WLCSP81), STM32L562 / VET6 (LQFP100), STM32L / 562QEI6Q (UFBGA132) and STM32L562ZET6Q (LQFP144). Markings vary with the supply chain. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample notice, are not qualified and not for production use.

The ordering code's temperature suffix fixes the guaranteed ambient temperature at full dissipation and the maximum junction temperature; working out the real dissipation and TJ shows which range an application needs. Worked case one: TAmax = 82 °C, IDDmax = 50 mA at VDD = 3.5 V, twenty outputs low at 8 mA and 0.4 V, eight outputs low at 20 mA and 1.3 V: PINTmax = 175 mW, PIOmax = 272 mW, PDmax = 447 mW; in LQFP100 (49.3 °C/W) TJmax = 82 + 22.04 = 104.04 °C, inside suffix 6 (TJ up to 105 °C). At that dissipation suffix 6 allows TAmax = 105 - 22.03 = 82.97 °C and suffix 3 allows 130 - 22.03 = 107.97 °C. Worked case two: TAmax = 100 °C, IDDmax = 20 mA at 3.5 V, twenty outputs low at 8 mA and 0.4 V: PINTmax = 70 mW, PIOmax = 64 mW, PDmax = 134 mW; in LQFP100 TJmax = 100 + 6.6 = 106.6 °C, above suffix 6, so suffix 3 is needed unless the dissipation comes down.

packages.name: LQFP48 7 x 7 mm, 0.5 mm pitch
notes: Recommended footprint: 0.50 mm pitch, pads 0.30 × 1.20 mm, 9.70 mm across the outer pad ends and 7.30 mm across the inner ends, pad rows 5.80 mm long.
The gauge plane is 0.25 mm above the seating plane.

packages.name: UFQFPN48 7 x 7 mm, 0.5 mm pitch
notes: Pin 1 corner chamfer C 0.500 × 45°; terminal corner radius R 0.125 typ.
Every lead and pad is soldered to the board for solder-joint life; the exposed pad on the underside is soldered to board ground.
